passage:
Monday, first week: Jeevan made a deal with himself. The new detective series would play only on his phone, only on the gym treadmill. He watched episode one while running and walked home sweaty and pleased.
Thursday, three weeks later: rain, a long meeting, a sore shoulder. "I'll watch just one at home and go tomorrow," he told his flatmate Rashmi, stretching out on the sofa. One became three. The next day he did go, but the episode he'd saved was already watched, so he left after ten minutes.
Sunday, a month in: Rashmi found him on episode nine, gym bag untouched by the door. "Weren't these gym-only?" He rubbed his face. "They were. Now they're just... mine." That night he signed out of the account on the TV.

qa.q: What did Jeevan tell Rashmi on the rainy Thursday?
qa.a: "I'll watch just one at home and go tomorrow."

qa.q: Why did watching at home on Thursday feel reasonable to Jeevan?
qa.a: He was tired, sore and rained on, and one episode seemed a small reward with the gym only postponed; the promise of tomorrow made the exception feel harmless.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what choice could have protected the plan?
qa.a: The Thursday exception, when the series left the gym; keeping the episodes locked to the treadmill even on bad days, or skipping both, would have kept their pull.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see Jeevan's slide from the gym to the sofa?
qa.a: Rashmi sees the gym bag sitting untouched by the door and asks one simple question that helps Jeevan admit the series has stopped being a reward.

grounding: An adult's series-and-gym pairing collapses once the series is watched outside the gym.

passage: Sit, Simran, I'll tell you about my famous cycling-and-radio plan, from when I was about your age in Goa. I loved a Sunday radio drama, and I thought, clever me, I'll only listen while pedalling the exercise cycle on the verandah. First two weeks, marvellous. I pedalled like a postman. Then one Sunday my knees felt lazy and I thought, I'll listen from the chair, just today, and cycle later. You know what happened to later. By the end of that month I knew every twist of the drama, and the cycle had my washing hanging on it. My mother laughed at me: "Maria, the drama was meant to pull you to the cycle, not replace it." So when you tell me your gym show is gym-only, keep it gym-only, child. Even on lazy days.

qa.q: Where did Maria plan to listen to the Sunday radio drama?
qa.a: Only while pedalling the exercise cycle on the verandah.

qa.q: What was Maria thinking on the lazy Sunday that changed everything?
qa.a: Maria thought listening from the chair "just today" and cycling later was a harmless swap, not seeing that later would never come once the reward was already enjoyed.

qa.q: What choice does Maria urge Simran to make, and why?
qa.a: To keep the gym show strictly for the gym even on lazy days, because once the treat is enjoyed elsewhere it stops pulling you to the task.

qa.q: How might Simran take this story about the cycle covered in washing?
qa.a: Simran may laugh, but may also recognise the same risk in the gym-only show; hearing it as a funny memory makes the warning easier to accept than a lecture.

grounding: An elder recalls how a radio-and-cycling pairing turned into listening without cycling once the pleasure was no longer reserved.

passage: Anjali had a rule: the cooking drama only at the gym, on her tablet, while she used the cross-trainer. It worked for a month. Then quarter-end hit her accounts team, and she was leaving the office after nine. The gym closed at ten. On the first late night she opened the tablet on the bus "just to see how the episode starts", telling herself she would save the rest. She got off with the episode finished and the gym already dark. By Friday she had watched four more on the bus and hadn't touched the cross-trainer. Joseph, her husband, noticed she was chatty about the show and oddly quiet about the gym. "Still gym-only, that drama?" he asked lightly. Anjali looked at the tablet. "More like bus-only now."

qa.q: What time did the gym close?
qa.a: At ten.

qa.q: Why did opening the tablet on the bus seem fine to Anjali?
qa.a: With late nights and no time for the gym, she told herself she would only watch the start; it felt like a small comfort rather than breaking the rule.

qa.q: Given the quarter-end crunch, what could Anjali choose instead?
qa.a: Pause the drama during busy weeks, or pair it with a short workout at home, rather than letting the bus become its new home.

qa.q: How does Joseph read Anjali's mood about the show and the gym?
qa.a: Joseph notices she is chatty about the drama but quiet about the gym and suspects the pairing has slipped, so he asks a light question instead of lecturing.

grounding: Under time pressure, an adult's drama-for-the-gym pairing turns into the drama without the gym.

passage: Anirban lived alone in a rented flat in Salt Lake, Kolkata, and in March he made a clever plan: the new spy series would play only on his phone, only on the gym treadmill. For two weeks it worked beautifully. Then came a Tuesday of pouring rain. "Just one episode on the sofa," he told himself. "I'll run double tomorrow." He watched three. On Thursday he was tired, so he watched on the metro home. By Sunday he'd finished the season, and his gym card showed one visit in ten days. His friend Rupam messaged: "Gym tomorrow?" Anirban stared at the finished season. There was nothing left to run toward. "Maybe next week," he typed, and felt oddly flat.

qa.q: How many visits did Anirban's gym card show in ten days?
qa.a: His gym card showed one visit in ten days.

qa.q: Why did 'Just one episode on the sofa' feel reasonable to Anirban that Tuesday?
qa.a: Rain and tiredness made the gym feel hard, and promising to run double tomorrow made breaking the rule feel like borrowing, not quitting.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what could Anirban do with the next series?
qa.a: The rainy Tuesday when the series left the treadmill; next time Anirban could keep episodes strictly for the gym, even on bad days, so the show still pulls him there.

qa.q: What might Rupam pick up from Anirban's reply?
qa.a: Rupam may sense from the flat 'Maybe next week' that the gym plan has faded, without knowing that the series used to be what got Anirban there.

grounding: An adult pairs a series with the gym, then lets it spill onto the sofa and the metro, finishes the season and stops going.

passage:
"Rehana Apa, you're home early. Isn't Thursday gym day?"
"It is. Was." Rehana dropped her bag and reached for the laptop. "Just one episode first."
"The baking show? You said that was only for the treadmill."
"I did. Then last week I watched one at home because my knee was sore. Then another because it was raining."
Her younger sister Zainab sat on the arm of the sofa. "How many gym days this month?"
"Two." Rehana winced. "And I'm on episode nineteen."
"So the show isn't pulling you to the gym anymore. It's replacing it."
"Don't be clever, Zainab." A pause. "Okay. You're right."
"Leave the laptop with me on gym days. You watch on your phone, at the gym."
Rehana hesitated, then slid the laptop across.

qa.q: Which episode was Rehana on?
qa.a: Rehana was on episode nineteen.

qa.q: Why does Rehana wince when she says 'Two'?
qa.a: She is embarrassed; the show was meant to get her to the gym, and admitting only two visits shows how far the plan has slipped.

qa.q: What choice at the end could make the bundle work again?
qa.a: Leaving the laptop with Zainab on gym days and watching only at the gym, so the show is reserved for the treadmill again.

qa.q: How does Zainab see what has happened to the plan?
qa.a: Zainab sees clearly that the show has turned from a reward into a replacement, and cares enough to say so and offer practical help, even at the risk of sounding clever.

grounding: An adult who paired a show with the gym now watches it at home instead, and her sister helps her reserve it again.
